1.pericope_label: The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?... one thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after

schools.summary: Set the phrase in literary and lexical history: Ellicott notes the thought 'appears nowhere else so grandly', traces the Vulgate's rendering to the Oxford motto, corrects strength to 'defence or bulwark', decides the flesh-eaters are warriors and not calumniators, and lays out the referents of 'in this' without choosing; Delitzsch hears 'the same longing after Zion' as the preceding psalm and notes the sanctuary is still only a tent though called a palace 'on account of Him who sits enthroned therein'.

Calvin has David rehearsing 'the desires and meditations with which he had exercised himself in the midst of his great dangers', the thanksgivings showing the psalm 'was composed after his deliverance'; Gill refers the light to Christ, 'the light of the world', not to nature or prosperity.

Clarke sets verse 2 at a battle where 'the Philistine lost his own life', expounds the pavilion literally from the butterfly the tent resembles, and leans away from the Davidic occasion toward the captivity, making verse 6 a national hope; Wesley reduces the opening to office — 'my counsellor in all my difficulties' — and hears behind the tabernacle 'the ancient custom of offenders, who used to flee to the tabernacle or altar'.

Henry hears a borrowed light, David shining 'as the moon does'; Spurgeon presses the possessive and the copula — God does not merely give light, 'he is light' — and turns the one thing desired into a rule, since 'divided aims tend to distraction, weakness, disappointment'.

Augustine reads the psalm as 'Christ's young soldier' speaking at his coming to the faith, and turns the devouring of flesh into a benefit: the guilty come near so that 'with their reviling tooth they may consume not me, but rather my fleshly desires'.

debates.question: What occasion does the psalm belong to?

positions.view: The words 'more naturally belong to the captivity' — verse 6 being a national hope of return.

debates.question: Are the flesh-eaters warriors or slanderers?

positions.view: Warriors: Job would allow the figure for calumniators, 'but the context marks out the situation so clearly as that of a warrior'.
Neither, in effect — their reviling consumes only 'my fleshly desires'.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the psalm as a catechumen's, and to turn the enemies' attack into a benefit.

themes: The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell.
Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: though war should rise against me, in this will I be confident.
One thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the Lord, and to enquire in his temple.
For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock.
And now shall mine head be lifted up above mine enemies round about me: therefore will I offer in his tabernacle sacrifices of joy; I will sing, yea, I will sing praises unto the Lord.

7.pericope_label: Hear, O Lord, when I cry with my voice... when my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me up

schools.summary: Explain or exploit the change of key: Ellicott takes it as evidence that vv.7-12 'are interpolated from another song of quite another kind in contents, art, and period', and elsewhere prunes single words — 'far' is 'unnecessary and misleading'; Delitzsch accounts for the same shift psychologically, since the reality 'overcome and surmounted by his faith' in the first part 'makes itself consciously felt here'.

Gill allows that God sometimes 'seems to turn a deaf ear', yet always proves 'a God hearing prayer'; he denies any literal forsaking by David's parents, reading it 'of something supposed yet to come' with the parents standing for closest friends and allies.

Clarke rejects the Authorised rendering of v.8 as 'forcibly extracted' and offers his own with the heart addressed rather than speaking, collects Persian parallels for the reciprocal turning of faces, and takes v.10 as past and factual; Wesley reads the putting away as exclusion 'from thy face or presence, or from the place of thy worship'.

Henry keeps the change circumstantial — cut off from the house of the Lord, David 'can find a way to the throne of grace by prayer' — and grounds the answer in God's goodness, not merit; Spurgeon figures the movement as a pendulum swinging 'from prayer to praise' and distinguishes true prayer from the Pharisee's, for whom being heard of men suffices.

debates.question: Why does the tone change at v.7?

positions.view: Because vv.7-12 come from a different song altogether.
Because the danger surmounted by faith in the first part now presses on the consciousness.
Because prayer and praise alternate in a life of faith.
The heart is addressed, not speaking: 'Unto thee, my heart, he hath said, Seek ye my face' — and corporately, God speaking to his Church.
The margin restores the Hebrew order, but the Authorised text 'really gives its meaning'.

debates.question: Did David's parents in fact forsake him?

positions.view: Yes, and already: 'my father and my mother have forsaken me; but the Lord hath gathered me up'.
No — the verse is hypothetical and the parents stand for his nearest friends and allies.

outliers.view: The only voice to treat the psalm as composite, assigning vv.7-12 to another poem of another period.

themes: Hear, O Lord, when I cry with my voice: have mercy also upon me, and answer me.
When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, Lord, will I seek.
Hide not thy face far from me; put not thy servant away in anger: thou hast been my help; leave me not, neither forsake me, O God of my salvation.
When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me up.

11.pericope_label: Teach me thy way, O Lord, and lead me in a plain path... wait on the Lord: be of good courage

schools.summary: Face the broken syntax of v.13 head on: Delitzsch holds an apodosis is 'wanting to the protasis', supplied only by the Greek and the Targum; Ellicott proposes emendation instead — 'by slightly changing a letter, we avoid the awkward ellipse' — and corrects the last verse to 'let thy heart be strong' and 'wait for Jehovah, and wait for Jehovah'.

Gill ranks the deliverances feared, being given over to one's own lusts being worse than falling among men 'whose tender mercies are cruel', catalogues the occasions of fainting, and lists what waiting means in practice.

Clarke argues that the supplied words 'I had fainted' 'injure the sense' and that the verse is an aposiopesis, comparing Neptune's unfinished threat to the winds; on the last verse he makes David the example rather than the exhorter and borrows the Vulgate's act like a man; Wesley supplies the double motive of the prayer for guidance.

Spurgeon takes the fainting as fact — 'even he who slew Goliath was subject to its attacks' — reverses the verbs into 'we must believe to see, not see to believe', and builds waiting into four postures, at the door, the foot, the table and the window.

debates.question: What is wrong with the syntax of v.13, and how should it be repaired?

positions.view: A word is missing: the apodosis must be supplied, as the Greek and Targum do.
Nothing is missing: the break is deliberate, an aposiopesis that the English supplement 'injures'.
The text is corrupt: change a letter and the ellipse disappears.

debates.question: What does waiting on the Lord involve?

positions.view: Four postures — 'wait at his door with prayer; wait at his foot with humility; wait at his table with service; wait at his window with expectancy'.
The service of a servant and the persistence of a beggar who 'take repulses and wait'.
Imitation of David: 'take me for an example. I waited on him, and he strengthened my heart.'

outliers.view: Alone in defending the broken sentence as a rhetorical figure rather than a defect to be mended.

themes: Teach me thy way, O Lord, and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies.
Deliver me not over unto the will of mine enemies: for false witnesses are risen up against me, and such as breathe out cruelty.
I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.
Wait on the Lord: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the Lord.
